# Stomach

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Internal medicine > Gastroenterology > Basics of gastroenterology > Stomach*

[Original Article Link](/library/U60b4S)

---

## Summary

The stomach is a hollow <u>intraperitoneal organ</u> in the <u>left upper quadrant</u> of the abdomen, between the <u>esophagus</u> and the <u>duodenum</u> in the <u>gastrointestinal tract</u>. It is supplied with arterial blood from the <u>celiac trunk</u> and its branches. The <u>veins of the stomach</u> drain into the <u>portal vein</u>, and the <u>lymphatics</u> eventually drain into the <u>celiac lymph nodes</u>. It is innervated by the <u>sympathetic and parasympathetic nervous system</u>, as well as the <u>myenteric plexus</u> and <u>submucous plexus</u> of the <u>enteric nervous system</u>. The stomach has four histological layers: the <u>mucosa</u>, <u>submucosa</u>, muscularis propria, and serosa. The <u>mucosa</u> is lined with numerous glands containing specialized cells that produce various secretions: e.g., <u>parietal cells</u>, which secrete <u>gastric acid</u> and <u>intrinsic factor</u>, and <u>gastric chief cells</u>, which secrete <u>pepsinogen</u>. <u>Acetylcholine</u> (<u>ACh</u>), <u>gastrin</u>, and <u>histamine</u> are the main stimulators of <u>gastric secretions</u>. <u>Somatostatin</u>, <u>cholecystokinin</u> (<u>CCK</u>), <u>secretin</u>, and <u>gastric inhibitory peptide</u> (<u>GIP</u>) are the main inhibitors.

## Gross anatomy

### Overview [[1]](/library/ES08Yf)




* Characteristics

* Hollow, muscular organ

* First intra-abdominal part of the <u>gastrointestinal tract</u>, situated between the <u>esophagus</u> (proximally) and the <u>duodenum</u> (distally)

* Divided into the <u>cardia</u>, <u>gastric fundus</u>, <u>body (stomach)</u>, and <u>pylorus</u>

* Location

* <u>LUQ</u> of the abdomen

* Abdominal regions: epigastric, left hypochondriac, and umbilical

* <u>Anterior</u> to the stomach

* <u>Anterior abdominal wall</u>

* Left lobe of the <u>liver</u>

* <u>Greater omentum</u>

* <u>Diaphragm</u>

* <u>Posterior</u> to the stomach

* <u>Spleen</u>

* Tail of the <u>pancreas</u>

* Left <u>kidney</u>

* Left <u>adrenal gland</u>

* <u>Transverse colon</u>

* Transverse mesocolon and <u>lesser sac</u>

* Function

* <u>Mechanical digestion</u> via <u>peristalsis</u>

* <u>Chemical digestion</u> via secretion of <u>gastric acid</u> and digestive enzymes

* Secretion of <u>intrinsic factor</u>





![Abdominal organs](media/czi6xqznu4e7wsvr6uwj58y2.jpg)

Abdominal organs




### Anatomical parts




* Sections of the stomach 

* Cardia: the part of the stomach that lies immediately <u>distal</u> to the <u>gastroesophageal sphincter</u>

* Gastric fundus: the dome-shaped region of the stomach just <u>lateral</u> to the <u>cardia</u>

* Body (stomach): the main portion of the stomach that lies between the fundus and the <u>pylorus</u>

* Pylorus: the terminal conical narrowing of the stomach that can be further subdivided into the <u>proximal</u> antrum and the <u>distal</u> pyloric canal

* Curvatures of the stomach

* Lesser curvature: the <u>medial</u> <u>concave</u> border of the stomach

* Greater curvature: the <u>lateral</u> <u>convex</u> border of the stomach

* Sphincters of the stomach

* Gastroesophageal sphincter (<u>lower esophageal sphincter</u>)

* Circular muscle located at the junction between the <u>gastric cardia</u> and <u>esophagus</u> (Th11)

* Prevents reflux of gastric contents into the <u>esophagus</u>

* Pyloric sphincter 

* A muscular ring located in the <u>pyloric canal</u>

* Controls the movement of gastric contents into the <u>duodenum</u>





> [!NOTE]
> The <u>antrum</u> and lower <u>lesser curvature</u> are the most common sites for peptic <u>stomach ulcers</u>.

### <u>Peritoneal</u> attachments




The stomach is an <u>intraperitoneal organ</u>.




* <u>Omentum</u>: extends from stomach (and <u>proximal</u> <u>duodenum</u>) to other abdominal organs

* <u>Greater omentum</u>: from <u>greater curvature</u> and covers intestines

* <u>Lesser omentum</u>: from <u>lesser curvature</u> to <u>liver</u>

* <u>Peritoneal ligaments</u> of the stomach 

* <u>Gastrohepatic ligament</u>

* <u>Gastrocolic ligament</u>

* <u>Gastrosplenic ligament</u>

#### <u>Veins</u>




* <u>Veins of the stomach</u>

* Right and left gastric veins

* Right and <u>left gastroepiploic veins</u>

* <u>Short gastric veins</u>

* Drain into <u>portal vein</u>

* The <u>anastomosis</u> between the <u>left gastric vein</u> and the esophageal <u>vein</u> is a site of <u>portosystemic anastomosis</u>.





> [!NOTE]
> <u>Esophageal varices</u> develop in <u>portal hypertension</u> due to the <u>portosystemic shunting</u> of blood from the <u>left gastric vein</u> (portal system) into the esophageal <u>veins</u> (caval system).

#### Innervation




| <u>Innervation of the stomach</u> |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  |  | Name | Effects |
| <u>Autonomic nervous system</u> | <u>Sympathetic</u> | <br>* <u>Celiac ganglion</u><br><br> | <br><br>* ↓ Glandular secretion<br><br>* ↓ <u>Peristalsis</u><br><br>* ↑ Sphincter tone<br><br><br> |
| <u>Parasympathetic</u> | <br>* <u>Vagus nerves</u><br><br> | <br><br>* ↑ Glandular secretion<br><br>* ↑ <u>Peristalsis</u><br><br>* ↓ Sphincter tone (i.e., sphincter relaxation)<br><br><br> |  |
| <u>Enteric nervous system</u> |  | <br>* <u>Submucous plexus</u> (<u>Meissner plexus</u>)<br><br> | <br>* Controls local gastrointestinal secretion and <u>nutrient</u> absorption<br><br> |
| <br>* <u>Myenteric plexus</u> (<u>Auerbach plexus</u>)<br><br> | <br>* Controls inherent myogenic motility of the <u>GIT</u><br><br> |  |  |





> [!NOTE]
> The left <u>vagus nerve</u> is <u>anterior</u> to the stomach, and the right vagus is <u>posterior</u> to it. This can be remembered with the mnemonic LARP: Left Anterior, Right Posterior.

## Microscopic anatomy

* The stomach's four histological layers are the same as the <u>layers of the gastrointestinal tract</u>.

* The <u>mucosa</u> of the stomach is specialized in the following ways: 

* It contains millions of gastric pits that are lined by mucus-secreting cells (foveolar cells) and open into one or more gastric glands.

* Gastric glands in the <u>lamina propria</u> contain various specialized cells and vary in composition and thickness depending on their location in the stomach.

* <u>Stem cells</u> located at the necks of the gastric glands proliferate and differentiate to replace gastric cells.

* <u>Enteroendocrine cells</u> are located throughout the gastric <u>mucosa</u> and secrete various <u>secretory and regulatory products of the gastrointestinal tract</u>.





| <br>Specialized cells of the gastric glands<br> |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Region | Cell type |  | Secretory product or function |
| <br>Fundus and body <br> | <br>* Chief cell<br><br>* Pyramid-shaped cells with basally located <u>nuclei</u> and <u>basophilic</u> <u>cytoplasm</u><br><br>* Contain <u>pepsinogen</u> granules<br><br>* Typically located at the bases of the gastric glands<br><br> |  | <br>* Pepsinogen<br><br> |
| <br>* Parietal cell<br><br>* Large eosinophilic cells with a circular <u>nucleus</u> (fried egg appearance)<br><br>* Typically located in the middle of the gastric glands<br><br> |  | <br><br>* <u>HCl</u><br><br>* <u>Intrinsic factor</u><br><br><br> |  |
| <br>* Enterochromaffin-like cell (<u>ECL cell</u>)<br><br>* A type of <u>neuroendocrine cell</u><br><br>* Adjacent to <u>parietal cells</u><br><br> |  | <br>* <u>Histamine</u><br><br> |  |
| <br>* P/D1 cell<br><br>* A type of <u>enteroendocrine cell</u><br><br>* Most abundant in glands of the <u>gastric fundus</u><br><br> |  | <br>* <u>Ghrelin</u> [[2]](/library/nPY726)<br><br> |  |
| <br><u>Pylorus</u> and <u>antrum</u> <br> | <br>* <u>D cell</u><br><br> |  | <br>* <u>Somatostatin</u><br><br> |
| <br>* <u>G cell</u><br><br> |  | <br>* <u>Gastrin</u><br><br> |  |

## Function

### Types of digestion




* Mechanical digestion: <u>peristalsis</u> of the stomach against a closed <u>pyloric sphincter</u>  → breakdown of food into smaller particles

* Chemical digestion: enzymatic breakdown of food into chyme (a semifluid mixture of digested food and digestive enzymes) by <u>gastric acid</u> and enzymes





See “<u>Secretory and regulatory products of the gastrointestinal tract</u>.”




### Mechanism of <u>gastric acid</u> secretion




* <u>Gastric acid</u> is secreted by the <u>parietal cells</u>.

* H<sup>+</sup>/K<sup>+</sup>-ATPase pump on the apical <u>cell membrane</u> of <u>parietal cells</u> secretes H<sup>+</sup> ions into the lumen.

* <u>Carbonic anhydrase</u> in <u>parietal cell</u> <u>cytoplasm</u> converts CO<sub>2</sub> into H<sup>+</sup> and <u>HCO<sub>3</sub><sup>-</sup></u>.

* Intracellular <u>HCO<sub>3</sub><sup>-</sup></u> is exchanged for <u>Cl<sup>-</sup></u> through the basolateral membrane.

* H<sup>+</sup> and <u>Cl<sup>-</sup></u> are secreted into the gastric lumen as <u>HCl</u>.





> [!NOTE]
> <u>Gastric acid</u> contains high amounts of <u>hydrochloric acid</u> (<u>HCl</u>). Repeated <u>vomiting</u> can therefore cause <u>metabolic alkalosis</u> due to the loss of acid (H<sup>+</sup>).




![Gastric acid secretion](media/ejs1pwpjhmpja99twfneedr9.jpg)

Gastric acid secretion




#### Phases




| <br>Phases of gastric acid secretion [[3]](/library/NlY-C6) |  |  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | Stimuli | Main mediators | Mechanism | Effect on acid secretion | Effect on gastric <u>pH</u> |
| Cephalic phase | <br>* Thought, <u>smell</u>, and <u>taste</u> of food<br><br> | <br>* <u>ACh</u> (<u>vagus nerve</u>)<br><br> | <br><br>* Stimulation of <u>parietal cells</u> to secrete <u>gastric acid</u><br><br>* Stimulation of <u>G cells</u> to secrete <u>gastrin</u> → stimulation of <u>parietal cells</u> to secrete <u>stomach acid</u><br><br>* Inhibition of <u>somatostatin</u><br><br><br> | <br>* Increase in acid secretion<br><br> | <br>* Decreases<br><br> |
| Gastric phase | <br>* Distention of the stomach by food<br><br> | <br><br>* <u>ACh</u> (<u>vagus nerve</u>)<br><br>* <u>Gastrin</u> (<u>G cells</u>)<br><br>* <u>Histamine</u> (<u>ECL cells</u>)<br><br><br> | <br><br>* Direct stimulation of <u>parietal cells</u> to secrete <u>gastric acid</u><br><br>* Stimulation of <u>G cells</u> to secrete <u>gastrin</u>, which stimulates:<br><br>* <u>Parietal cells</u> to secrete more acid directly<br><br>* <u>Enterochromaffin cells</u> to release <u>histamine</u>, which stimulates <u>parietal cells</u> to secrete more acid<br><br><br> | <br>* Increases (food buffers <u>gastric acid</u>)<br><br> |  |
| Intestinal phase | <br>* Acidic <u>chyme</u> containing <u>peptides</u> and lipid metabolites enters <u>duodenum</u><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Cholecystokinin</u> (<u>I cells</u>)<br><br>* <u>Secretin</u> (<u>S cells</u>)<br><br>* <u>Gastric inhibitory peptide</u> (<u>K cells</u>)<br><br>* <u>Somatostatin</u> (<u>D cells</u>)<br><br><br> | <br>* Stimulation of <u>CCK</u>, <u>secretin</u>, and <u>GIP</u> release (feedback regulatory <u>hormones</u>) → inhibition of further <u>gastric acid</u> secretion<br><br> | <br>* Decrease in acid secretion<br><br> | <br>* Decreases (food moves into the <u>duodenum</u> → buffering of acid by food decreases)<br><br> |

#### Disturbances of <u>gastric secretions</u>




| Most important conditions that cause disturbances in <u>gastric acid</u> secretion |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
|  | Condition | Pathomechanism |
| Increased <u>gastric acid</u> secretion | <br>* <u>Helicobacter pylori</u> <u>gastritis</u><br><br> | <br><br>* ↑ <u>Gastrin</u> secretion<br><br>* ↓ Protective factors/mucous production<br><br><br> |
| <br>* <u>Zollinger-Ellison</u> syndrome (<u>gastrinoma</u>)<br><br> | <br>* <u>Parietal cell</u> hyperstimulation<br><br> |  |
| <br>* <u>NSAIDs</u><br><br> | <br>* ↓ Protective <u>prostaglandin</u> secretion<br><br> |  |
| <br>Decreased <u>gastric acid</u> secretion (achlorhydria) | <br>* <u>Autoimmune gastritis</u><br><br> | <br>* <u>Antibodies</u> against <u>parietal cells</u><br><br> |
| <br>* <u>H2 antihistamines</u><br><br> | <br>* Reversible inhibition of <u>H2 histamine receptors</u> on <u>parietal cells</u><br><br> |  |
| <br>* <u>Proton pump inhibitors</u> (<u>PPIs</u>)<br><br> | <br>* <u>Irreversible inhibition</u> of <u>H<sup>+</sup>/K<sup>+</sup>-ATPase</u> in <u>parietal cells</u> → complete suppression of <u>gastric acid</u> secretion<br><br> |  |

* See “<u>Embryology of the gastrointestinal tract</u>.”

## Clinical significance

* Pathology

* <u>Peptic ulcer disease</u> (<u>PUD</u>)

* <u>Autoimmune gastritis</u>, <u>vitamin B12 deficiency</u> (<u>pernicious anemia</u>)

* <u>Hypertrophic pyloric stenosis</u>

* <u>Hiatal hernia</u>

* <u>Congenital diaphragmatic hernias</u>

* <u>Atrophic gastritis</u>

* <u>Gastrinoma</u> (<u>Zollinger-Ellison syndrome</u>)

* <u>Ménétrier disease</u>

* <u>Gastric cancer</u>

* <u>MALT lymphoma</u>

* Pharmacology

* <u>Proton pump inhibitors</u>

* <u>H2 antihistamines</u>
